title: The raft
hookLine: the raft is for crossing, not for carrying on your head afterward (MN 22)

lines: A RAFT OF GRASS AND STICKS.
SHOULDN'T I TAKE IT WITH ME?
cards: A man on a long journey comes to a wide stretch of water. On this side, danger. On the far side, safety.
No ferry, no bridge. So he gathers grass, sticks, branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddles across with his hands and feet. He makes it.
Standing on the far bank, the dripping raft at his feet, he has a thought: this raft was so useful to me. Shouldn't I take it with me?

teach.b: It's the same discourse as yesterday's water snake, MN 22. The Buddha asks the monks: if the man lifted the raft onto his head and carried it wherever he went, would he be doing what should be done with a raft?
No, they say. Then the Buddha gives the answer himself: haul it up onto dry land, or leave it floating in the water, and go on your way.
I have taught you the teaching as a raft, he says, for crossing over, not for holding on to.

teach.h: LET GO EVEN OF GOOD THINGS.
teach.b: And he adds a line read in more than one way: understanding the simile of the raft, you should let go even of good things, how much more so of bad things.
The Pali word is dhamma, which can mean the teaching, or good states and qualities. Some read the line as: even the teaching is let go once it has done its work.
The old commentary reads it as: let go even of attachment to calm and insight. Both say: don't cling.
Neither says: throw the raft away before you've crossed.

The man is on the far bank when he sets it down; in the middle of the river, you hold on and paddle. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: “Few are there among men who arrive at the other shore.”
And the week looks back: what you think about often, the finer peg, the last resort, the saw, Lady Vedehika, alagadda, and the raft. Seven pictures, each one meant to be used.

how: The raft simile is taught in Theravada, Zen and Tibetan settings as a reminder that practices and doctrines are means, not ends.

o: a ferry the monks ran across the Ganges
a teaching used to cross, then set down
a boat the Buddha kept for his journeys

games.q: match the pieces of the raft.

s: the raft simile means you can drop the teaching before you've crossed
the man sets it down on the far bank, not mid-river.
the raft is in the same discourse as the water snake
the monks say he should carry the raft on his head
they say no; then the Buddha says to leave it on land or in the water and go on.

games.q: you've crossed the river on your homemade raft. what does the Buddha say to do with it?
o: carry it on your head; it was so useful
leave it on the bank or in the water, and go on
burn it so nobody else can use it
games.why: leave it and go on. the teaching is for crossing, not for holding on to, and you only set it down once you're across.

practice: Think of one thing that once helped you across something: a habit, a routine, a belief about yourself, a way of coping that worked back then. Ask honestly whether you're still crossing, or already on the bank, carrying it.
If you're still crossing, keep paddling; if you're across, picture setting it down on dry ground, with thanks.

wordCard.voice: The raft. The teaching is for crossing over, not for carrying on your head once you're across.

orig.note: Pali kulla: a raft; the simile is called kullūpama, the raft simile.

carryVoice: Your line: put the raft down. Thanks for the raft, and then open hands. That's a week.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft)

sources.q: Few are there among men who arrive at the other shore
